modules.title: Refresh the language of maths
modules.purpose: Read equations comfortably and connect arithmetic to images before tackling neural networks.
lessons: 01 Images as numbers: scalars, vectors, matrices, shape and indexing
02 Functions and graphs: input, output, slope and composition
03 Sums, averages and squared error: reading sigma notation
04 Powers, logarithms and the sigmoid: confidence versus evidence
outcomes: Explain each symbol in an image transformation.
Evaluate and compose simple functions.
Compute a mean and a mean squared error by hand.
Use logarithms and exponentials without memorizing isolated formulas.
modules.reading: MML Chapter 1; CS205A 0.1 and 0.3.2. Use the supplied lessons first. Review the CS231n Python/NumPy tutorial if Python is unfamiliar.
modules.practice: For I=[[20,60],[100,140]], compute 0.5I+10 and its mean. For predictions [2,4] and targets [1,7], compute MSE. Sketch y=2x+1 and explain its slope.
modules.lab: Run the starter notebook. Create a toy grayscale image, change its brightness, normalize it, blend it with another image, and explain each array shape.
modules.gate: Without notes: explain scalar/vector/matrix, compute a four-pixel mean and an MSE, and distinguish scaling from adding an offset.
modules.artifact: A one-page explanation plus the completed Week 1-2 notebook.

modules.title: Vectors, geometry and linear maps
modules.purpose: Understand features, similarities and the transformations performed by a neural-network layer.
lessons: 05 Vectors as positions, displacements and features
06 Norms, dot products, angles and projections
07 Matrices as maps; multiplication and composition
08 Independence, bases, rank and null spaces
outcomes: Explain the geometric meaning of a dot product.
Track dimensions through matrix products.
Connect rank to information preserved or lost.
Separate elementwise multiplication from matrix multiplication.
modules.reading: MML 2.2 and 2.4-2.7; 3.1-3.5 and 3.8. CS205A 0.2-0.3. Optional: Guo Part I, Chapter 1, Sections 1-3.
modules.practice: For x=[1,2] and w=[3,-1], compute w dot x. Apply A=[[2,0],[0,1]] to x and describe the geometry. Find a nonzero vector mapped to zero by B=[[1,1],[2,2]].
modules.lab: Build a nearest-centroid classifier for synthetic 8x8 bars. Compare Euclidean distance and normalized dot-product similarity. Fit centroids using training data only.
modules.gate: Explain why a linear layer can change feature dimension and why matrix-product order matters. Solve three unseen shape questions.
modules.artifact: A shape-annotated forward pass and a similarity-classification notebook.

modules.title: Linear systems and least squares
modules.purpose: Learn how noisy measurements become a fitting problem and why stable solvers matter.
lessons: 09 Exact, inconsistent and underdetermined systems
10 Least squares as projection and residual minimization
11 QR, pseudoinverses and numerical conditioning
12 Regularization and the cost of overfitting
outcomes: Formulate a small fitting problem as Ax approximately b.
Explain residual orthogonality.
Explain why an explicit matrix inverse is usually a poor solving strategy.
Compare unregularized fitting and ridge fitting.
modules.reading: MML 2.1-2.3 and 3.8; preview 9.1-9.2. CS205A Chapters 2-4. CV Appendix A.2.
modules.practice: Fit y approximately ax+b to (0,1), (1,2), (2,2). Write A and b before computing. Derive A^T(Ax-b)=0 for least squares once Module 5 supplies the derivative tools; for now, explain the projection.
modules.lab: Fit a line to clean data, then add noise and one outlier. Compare residuals and coefficient changes. Use numpy.linalg.lstsq; do not invert A^T A.
modules.gate: State when the solution is unique, distinguish residual from measurement noise, and explain an ill-conditioned example.
modules.artifact: A fitting report with clean/noisy/outlier comparisons and limitations.

modules.title: Eigenvectors, SVD and PCA
modules.purpose: See how features can be compressed and why directions of variation matter.
lessons: 13 Eigenvectors and repeated linear transformations
14 SVD as geometry and low-rank structure
15 PCA: centering, covariance and projection
16 Reconstruction error and the dangers of data leakage
outcomes: Explain eigenvalues and singular values geometrically.
Construct a truncated SVD reconstruction.
Explain why PCA must center data.
Fit preprocessing on training data and apply it unchanged to validation data.
modules.reading: MML 4.2 and 4.4-4.6; 10.1-10.4 and 10.6. CS205A Chapters 5-6. CV 5.2.3 and Appendix A.1.
modules.practice: Find the eigenvalues of diag(3,1). For singular values [5,2,1], find the squared Frobenius reconstruction error after keeping the largest one. Explain why PCA directions are not class labels.
modules.lab: Compress one grayscale image at several ranks; compare storage and error. Apply training-fitted PCA before the nearest-centroid classifier.
modules.gate: Distinguish eigenvalues from singular values, show a rank-k reconstruction, and explain one case where compression harms recognition.
modules.artifact: An image-compression experiment and PCA baseline.

modules.title: Calculus for learning
modules.purpose: Understand derivatives as sensitivity and the chain rule as the engine of backpropagation.
lessons: 17 Limits, derivatives and local linearity
18 Partial derivatives, gradients and directional derivatives
19 Jacobians, chain rule and computational graphs
20 Hessians, Taylor approximation and finite-difference checks
outcomes: Derive basic scalar and multivariable derivatives.
Track Jacobian dimensions.
Differentiate a composed computation.
Check analytic gradients against finite differences.
modules.reading: MML 5.1-5.3 and 5.5-5.8; treat 5.4 as reference. CS205A 0.4 and 12.3. Learn simple integrals as areas for Module 6.
modules.practice: For L(w)=(3w-2)^2, find dL/dw and evaluate at w=1. For f(x,y)=x^2+3xy, compute its gradient. Verify a derivative using a central difference.
modules.lab: Build a scalar computational graph and a gradient checker. Sweep the finite-difference step to observe truncation and roundoff error.
modules.gate: Derive the gradient of a new two-stage expression, state its shape, and explain why the numerical check has a useful step-size range.
modules.artifact: A worked chain-rule derivation and a verified gradient-check utility.

modules.title: Probability, noise and uncertainty
modules.purpose: Understand what model probabilities mean and how noise changes the reliability of predictions.
lessons: 21 Events, conditional probability and Bayes theorem
22 Random variables, distributions and expectations
23 Variance, covariance and Gaussian noise
24 Sampling, confidence and empirical uncertainty
outcomes: Separate P(A given B) from P(B given A).
Distinguish a density from a probability.
Interpret covariance and correlation.
Explain why high accuracy on a tiny sample is weak evidence.
modules.reading: MML 6.1-6.5; defer 6.6-6.7. CV Appendix B.1 and B.4. Guo Part III, Chapter 4 is optional measure-theory enrichment, not the probability foundation.
modules.practice: Given P(A)=0.2, P(B given A)=0.8 and P(B given not A)=0.1, compute P(A given B). For pixel values [0,2,4], find mean and population variance. Integrate the uniform density on [0,1] over [0.2,0.5].
modules.lab: Generate noisy versions of the same synthetic image. Estimate pixel means and variances; use repeated trials to measure classifier accuracy variation.
modules.gate: Solve an unseen Bayes problem, compute a variance, and explain why a continuous variable can have nonzero density but zero probability at one exact value.
modules.artifact: A noise experiment with uncertainty estimates and a written interpretation.

modules.title: Statistical learning and losses
modules.purpose: Connect loss functions to assumptions about data, then build a transparent recognition baseline.
lessons: 25 Likelihood, maximum likelihood and negative log likelihood
26 Priors, MAP and regularization
27 Logistic regression, softmax and cross entropy
28 Train/validation/test splits, bias, variance and calibration
outcomes: Derive squared error from independent Gaussian residuals.
Explain the role of a prior.
Compute softmax and cross entropy stably.
Compare confidence, correctness and calibration.
modules.reading: MML 8.1-8.4 and 8.6; 9.1-9.2. CV 5.1.2-5.1.3, 5.3.3-5.3.4 and Appendix B.2-B.4. MML Chapter 12 is optional after the core.
modules.practice: For a correct-class probability of 0.8, compute -ln(0.8). Explain why predicting 0.99 for a wrong class incurs a large loss. Derive the softmax shift-invariance identity.
modules.lab: Train logistic or softmax regression on synthetic image vectors. Compare a linear model with a nearest-centroid baseline; reserve test data until the final comparison.
modules.gate: Explain the statistical assumption behind MSE and cross entropy and spot two examples of data leakage.
modules.artifact: A recognition baseline with losses, confusion matrix and split protocol.

modules.title: Optimization and reliable training
modules.purpose: Understand learning-rate choices, gradients, curvature and training failure modes.
lessons: 29 Gradient descent and optimality conditions
30 Mini-batch SGD, momentum and adaptive steps
31 Convexity, curvature and constrained problems
32 Initialization, scaling and optimization diagnostics
outcomes: Derive and apply a gradient-descent update.
Separate optimization failure from generalization failure.
Explain the difference between convex and nonconvex objectives.
Use learning curves to diagnose training behavior.
modules.reading: MML 7.1-7.3. CS205A Chapters 8-9; Chapter 10 optional. CV 5.3.6 and Appendix A.3.
modules.practice: For L(w)=(w-3)^2, start at w=0 and compute one step with learning rate 0.1. Derive the convergence range 0<learning rate<1 for this particular quadratic. Do not generalize that range to every loss.
modules.lab: Compare learning rates and momentum on a stretched quadratic and your linear classifier. Keep the data split and initialization controlled.
modules.gate: Explain a divergent run, derive an update without notes, and distinguish a stationary point from a guaranteed global minimum.
modules.artifact: An optimization experiment with justified settings and failure analysis.

modules.title: Images, convolution and frequency
modules.purpose: Build the mathematical picture behind filters and convolutional layers.
lessons: 33 Sampling, aliasing and image coordinates
34 Discrete convolution and cross-correlation
35 Padding, stride, channels and receptive fields
36 Fourier transforms, smoothing and edge responses
outcomes: Compute a filter response by hand.
Distinguish mathematical convolution from unflipped cross-correlation.
Calculate output shapes and receptive fields.
Connect smoothing and edge detection to frequency content.
modules.reading: CV 2.3.1, 3.2, 3.4 and 3.5; 5.4. MML 3.7 and complex-number reminders as needed. Read the indicated headings; do not read all of Chapter 3 at once.
modules.practice: For input length 7, kernel size 3, padding 1 and stride 2, compute output length. Convolve [1,2,3] with [1,1] in full mode. Explain why two adjacent objects can become indistinguishable after excessive downsampling.
modules.lab: Implement a small 2D cross-correlation using loops, compare it with a reference calculation, and test smoothing and edge kernels on synthetic images.
modules.gate: Get shapes correct for an unseen convolution layer and explain how weight sharing differs from a fully connected layer.
modules.artifact: A from-scratch filter notebook with an output-shape calculation sheet.

modules.title: Neural networks and backpropagation
modules.purpose: Derive a trainable network before relying on a deep-learning framework.
lessons: 37 Affine layers, activations and expressive power
38 Backpropagation through a two-layer network
39 Regularization, normalization and numerical stability
40 Framework autograd compared with your own gradients
outcomes: Write the forward pass with explicit batch and parameter shapes.
Derive weight and bias gradients.
Verify gradients numerically before training.
Explain why stacking linear layers without nonlinearities stays linear.
modules.reading: MML 5.6; CV 5.3.1-5.3.6. Optional CS231n neural-network case study; use current framework documentation when installing a framework.
modules.practice: For X of shape (N,D), W1=(D,H), W2=(H,C), give every activation and gradient shape. Derive dL/dW for Z=XW+b. Explain the sum over the batch in the bias gradient.
modules.lab: Implement a small NumPy MLP with stable softmax and mini-batch SGD. Overfit a tiny subset as a debugging check, then train and compare validation results.
modules.gate: Gradient checks pass away from nondifferentiable activation points, and you can explain every backward-pass operation.
modules.artifact: A small neural network with gradient checks and a training report.

modules.title: Recognition, detection and segmentation
modules.purpose: Understand how different vision tasks change the model outputs, objectives and evaluation.
lessons: 41 CNN classification, inductive bias and augmentation
42 Bounding boxes, localization losses and IoU
43 Pixel classification, segmentation and class imbalance
44 Precision/recall, thresholds, average precision and mask metrics
outcomes: Distinguish image labels, object boxes and pixel masks.
Compute box IoU and mask IoU.
Explain multi-part detection losses and pixelwise cross entropy.
Recognize when background-dominated accuracy is misleading.
modules.reading: CV 5.4 and 6.2-6.4. CS231n public notes or lectures are optional applied support. Framework versions and dataset choices are selected when the lab begins.
modules.practice: Two 2x2 boxes overlap over a 1x2 region: find their IoU. For TP=8, FP=2 and FN=4, compute precision and recall. Explain the failure of all-background predictions on a mostly background segmentation image.
modules.lab: Train a compact CNN on generated bars/rectangles. Add one-object box prediction or binary mask prediction, changing outputs and losses explicitly. This toy task teaches mechanics, not real-world performance.
modules.gate: Explain outputs, loss and metric for all three tasks, and justify one choice for class imbalance.
modules.artifact: A CNN experiment with either a localization or segmentation extension.

modules.title: Capstone and a route into research
modules.purpose: Use the maths to justify model choices, evaluate evidence and read a research method critically.
lessons: 45 Choose a question, dataset protocol and baseline
46 Compare models using controlled experiments
47 Audit errors, uncertainty and domain shift
48 Explain a paper and defend your mathematical decisions
outcomes: Run a reproducible baseline and one justified improvement.
Report meaningful metrics without tuning on the test set.
Analyze at least three failure examples.
Map a method description to its inputs, parameters, loss and assumptions.
modules.reading: Revisit CV Chapters 5-6 and the MML sections your project uses. Choose one original paper after discussing its prerequisites; do not treat a list of fashionable models as a reading assignment.
modules.practice: Write your hypothesis before training. Predict what changes when you alter one hyperparameter. Separate measured results from explanations that remain hypotheses.
modules.lab: Extend the synthetic recognition project, or choose a small public dataset when the module starts. Compare a linear baseline with an MLP or CNN; detection or segmentation is an optional extension, not a second mandatory capstone.
modules.gate: Deliver code, split protocol, seed, baseline, one controlled comparison, metrics, failure examples and a limitations section.
modules.artifact: A 3-5 page report, runnable experiment and a 10-minute mathematical explanation.

modules.title: Geometry of images and cameras
modules.purpose: Describe how points move between planes and cameras, then fit those maps robustly to noisy matches.
lessons: 49 Homogeneous coordinates and 2D transformations
50 Homographies, warping and resampling
51 The pinhole camera, rotations and calibration
52 Robust fitting: RANSAC and Gauss-Newton refinement
outcomes: Write translation, similarity, affine and projective maps as 3×3 matrices and say what each preserves.
Estimate a homography from four correspondences and warp an image with inverse mapping and bilinear sampling.
Project 3D points with K[R|t] and explain intrinsics, extrinsics and lens distortion.
Fit a model with RANSAC and refine it with Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt.
modules.reading: CV 2.1.1-2.1.5, 3.6.1, 8.1.1-8.1.4 and 11.1; Appendix A.3 and B.3. MML 3.9. Guo Part II, Chapter 1 and Part IV, Chapters 2-3 for geometric depth.
modules.practice: Map the point (2,1) with the homography H=[[1,0,1],[0,1,0],[0.5,0,1]] and divide by the last coordinate. Explain why parallel lines can meet after a homography. For 40% outliers and a 2-point line model, how many RANSAC samples give 99% confidence of one clean sample?
modules.lab: Pick four corners of a planar object in a photo, estimate H with the direct linear transform, and rectify the image with inverse mapping. Then add synthetic outlier matches and compare least squares with RANSAC.
modules.gate: Derive the two homography constraints from one correspondence, explain the role of the last coordinate, and justify a RANSAC threshold and iteration count.
modules.artifact: A rectification notebook with a robust homography estimate and a residual analysis.
modules.after: Take Lesson 49 any time after Module 02, Lesson 51 after Module 04 and Lesson 52 after Module 08.

modules.title: Matrix calculus and modern architectures
modules.purpose: Derive layer gradients in matrix form, compare distributions with entropy and KL divergence, and read attention and multi-scale networks as mathematics.
lessons: 53 Matrix calculus for layers and losses
54 Entropy, KL divergence and contrastive learning
55 Attention and vision transformers
56 Multi-scale features: pyramids, FPN and U-Net
outcomes: Derive gradients of linear layers and quadratic forms with their shapes, using the chain rule and trace identities.
Compute entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence, and explain label smoothing and the InfoNCE loss.
Compute scaled dot-product attention by hand and explain the √d scaling and positional information.
Relate Gaussian and Laplacian pyramids to feature pyramid networks, U-Net skip connections and anchors across scales.
modules.practice: Find the gradient of f(x)=xᵀAx for a non-symmetric A. Compute KL(p‖q) for p=(0.5,0.5) and q=(0.9,0.1), and KL(q‖p). Compute one row of softmax(QKᵀ/√d) for a query and two keys.
modules.lab: Implement one attention head in NumPy, check its gradients against finite differences, and visualize which image patches one query attends to. Then build a three-level Laplacian pyramid and reconstruct the image exactly.
modules.gate: Derive dL/dW for a linear layer from the scalar chain rule, explain why attention scores are divided by √d, and say what an FPN level adds that a single feature map lacks.
modules.artifact: An attention-and-pyramid notebook with gradient checks and a short written explanation.
modules.after: Take Lesson 53 any time after Module 05, Lesson 54 after Module 07, and Lessons 55-56 after Module 11.

modules.title: Local features, motion and tracking
modules.purpose: Find and describe distinctive points, measure how image content moves between frames, and follow objects over time with a Kalman filter.
lessons: 57 Image gradients, the structure tensor and corners
58 Scale space, descriptors and matching
59 Optical flow and direct image alignment
60 Multivariate Gaussians, Kalman filtering and data association
outcomes: Compute image gradients with derivative-of-Gaussian filters and classify a window as flat, edge or corner from its structure tensor.
Detect blobs at their characteristic scale and accept descriptor matches with the ratio and mutual-nearest-neighbour tests.
Solve Lucas–Kanade as a 2×2 least-squares problem, explain the aperture problem and recover large motion coarse-to-fine.
Derive the Kalman predict and update steps from Gaussian rules and assign detections to tracks with the Hungarian algorithm.
modules.practice: Compute the Harris response for a window with gradients (1,0),(1,0),(0,1),(0,1). Solve Lucas–Kanade for four pixels. Run one Kalman predict-update step by hand.
modules.lab: Map corners and gradient orientation on a photo, match features to a warped copy with a known homography, estimate optical flow on a synthetic warp, and track noisy boxes with a Kalman filter.
modules.gate: Explain why the eigenvalues of the structure tensor separate corners from edges, why Lucas–Kanade fails on a straight edge, and how a Kalman filter corrects a velocity it never measures.
modules.artifact: A features-and-tracking notebook: corner map, ratio-test precision curve, flow field and a tracked trajectory.
modules.after: Take Lessons 57-59 after Module 09 and Lesson 52; Lesson 60 after Module 06 and Lesson 42.

modules.title: Two-view geometry and neural rendering
modules.purpose: Relate two views of a scene, recover depth and camera motion, refine everything with bundle adjustment, and render novel views by integrating along rays.
lessons: 61 Epipolar geometry and the eight-point algorithm
62 Triangulation, rectification and stereo depth
63 Rotations as a manifold, point-set alignment and bundle adjustment
64 Volume rendering and neural radiance fields
outcomes: Derive the epipolar constraint, estimate the fundamental matrix with the normalised eight-point algorithm and recover pose from the essential matrix.
Triangulate points, compute disparity from a cost volume and propagate disparity error to depth.
Update rotations with the exponential map, align point sets with Kabsch and explain the Schur complement in bundle adjustment.
Render a pixel by alpha-compositing samples along a ray and explain why NeRF needs positional encoding.
modules.practice: Check the epipolar constraint for a sideways camera step. Triangulate one point and convert disparity 20 px to depth with f = 800 px and B = 0.1 m. Composite three samples along a ray.
modules.lab: Draw epipolar lines between two synthetic views, block-match a rectified stereo pair, align point sets with ICP and ray-march a small volumetric scene.
modules.gate: Explain why a planar scene or pure rotation makes the fundamental matrix degenerate, why depth error grows with the square of distance, and why occluded samples receive little gradient in volume rendering.
modules.artifact: A two-view notebook: estimated F with epipolar distances, a disparity map with depth error bars, and a rendered ray with its weights.
modules.after: Take Lessons 61-63 after Module 13 and Lesson 58; Lesson 64 after Lesson 51 and Module 09.

modules.title: Set prediction, generative models and splatting
modules.purpose: Read the mathematics behind DETR-style detectors, variational autoencoders, diffusion models and 3D Gaussian splatting.
lessons: 65 Cross-attention, positional encodings and set prediction
66 Latent-variable models: from EM to the variational autoencoder
67 Diffusion models: noising, denoising and sampling
68 3D Gaussian splatting
outcomes: Compute cross-attention and sinusoidal position encodings, and train a set predictor with a Hungarian-matched loss and GIoU.
Fit a Gaussian mixture with EM, derive the ELBO and explain the reparameterisation trick and the Gaussian KL term.
Derive closed-form forward noising, explain noise prediction as denoising and sample with DDPM, DDIM and guidance.
Project a 3D Gaussian to a 2D splat with the camera Jacobian and alpha-composite depth-sorted splats.
modules.reading: CV 5.5.3, 6.3.3, 6.4.2-6.4.3, 5.2.1-5.2.2, 5.5.4, 13.4. MML 6.5, 6.7, 11.1-11.4. Primary papers for diffusion and splatting are cited in the lessons.
modules.practice: Compute GIoU for two non-overlapping boxes. Compute GMM responsibilities and a Gaussian KL. Noise and denoise one value with known noise. Project one 3D Gaussian to a 2D covariance.
modules.lab: Match predicted boxes to targets with the Hungarian algorithm, fit a colour mixture with EM, sample 2D diffusion with DDPM and DDIM steps, and render a small set of Gaussian splats.
modules.gate: Explain why set prediction needs a matching step, why the ELBO is a lower bound, why predicting noise recovers the clean image, and why splats must be sorted by depth.
modules.artifact: A generative-models notebook: an EM log-likelihood curve, a diffusion sampling trajectory and a splatted image.
modules.after: Take Lesson 65 after Module 14; Lessons 66-67 after Lessons 54 and 60; Lesson 68 after Lessons 60 and 64.

MML.title: Mathematics for Machine Learning
MML.authors: Marc Peter Deisenroth, A. Aldo Faisal, Cheng Soon Ong
MML.edition: Cambridge University Press, 2020; downloaded draft dated 2024-01-15
MML.role: The main mathematical bridge. Read selected sections after the lesson.

CS205A.title: Mathematical Methods for Computer Vision, Robotics, and Graphics
CS205A.role: Selected numerical explanations: least squares, SVD, conditioning, optimization.

CV.title: Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications
CV.role: The application companion, especially Chapters 3, 5, 6 and Appendices A, B.

GUO.title: Modern Mathematics and Applications in Computer Graphics and Vision
GUO.role: Optional geometry enrichment. Most topology and manifold chapters come later.
